image.subject: In a wood-paneled practice room at the Shanghai Conservatory in 1966, Zhuli: A graceful 19-year-old Chinese violinist with fiery expressive dark eyes, hair tied back with a simple red ribbon, slender hands calloused from violin strings, wearing a modest dark cotton student dress, sits trembling on a piano bench clutching classical sheet music against her chest, while Kai: A charismatic 30-year-old Chinese pianist with sharp intense eyes, neat swept-back black hair, lean athletic frame, wearing a crisp dark wool tunic or pressed shirt, carrying an aura of guarded vigilance, stands tensely in the open doorway.

storyboard.claim: Kai confronts a terrified Zhuli inside her private conservatory practice room as political purges begin.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Dusty afternoon light in room 103 showing Zhuli holding sheet music close while Kai stands watchfully at the door.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Illustrates the previous discussion of artists being pressured to betray their craft.
storyboard.addedInformation: Establishes the physical intimacy and impending danger between the two young musicians.

image.subject: In a Shanghai Conservatory music room in 1966, Kai: A charismatic 30-year-old Chinese pianist with sharp intense eyes, neat swept-back black hair, lean athletic frame, wearing a crisp dark wool tunic or pressed shirt, carrying an aura of guarded vigilance, places a printed booklet of revolutionary marches by Xian Xinghai with a bright red cover onto a dark polished upright piano before Zhuli.

storyboard.claim: Kai offers Zhuli state-approved revolutionary scores by Xian Xinghai as a protective shield.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Kai's hands pressing the red-bound revolutionary march score onto the upright piano.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Develops Kai's attempted intervention from the preceding beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the stark visual contrast of state-mandated propaganda scores replacing classical sonatas.

image.subject: Inside the dimly lit Shanghai practice room in 1966, Kai: A charismatic 30-year-old Chinese pianist with sharp intense eyes, neat swept-back black hair, lean athletic frame, wearing a crisp dark wool tunic or pressed shirt, carrying an aura of guarded vigilance, leans forward urgently toward Zhuli: A graceful 19-year-old Chinese violinist with fiery expressive dark eyes, hair tied back with a simple red ribbon, slender hands calloused from violin strings, wearing a modest dark cotton student dress, warning her to abandon defiance.

storyboard.claim: Kai pleads with Zhuli to compromise her artistic ideals to stay alive under the new political regime.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Close framing on Kai's anxious, vigilant expression as he whispers urgent advice across the wooden music stand.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Elaborates on the safe music he brought in the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: Reveals Kai's pragmatism and terror versus Zhuli's unyielding artistic conscience.

image.subject: At a cluttered wooden work desk in Shanghai in 1966 beneath a hanging bare lightbulb, Sparrow: A slender 35-year-old Chinese man with sensitive thoughtful eyes, slightly disheveled dark hair, high cheekbones, wearing a plain buttoned cotton cadre jacket over a fraying white shirt, posture quiet and introspective, sits with a dipping fountain pen hesitantly scoring crude repetitive march melodies beside a gray metal propaganda loudspeaker.

storyboard.claim: Great composers like Sparrow are coerced into composing simplistic propaganda slogans for rallies.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Sparrow sitting under a harsh overhead lightbulb penning simplistic notes beside official directives.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Broadens Kai's warning to the wider fate of Conservatory composers like Sparrow.
storyboard.addedInformation: Visualizes the humiliation of genius reduced to formulaic party jingles.

storyboard.claim: Forcing musicians to mock their own sacred craft causes devastating cognitive dissonance.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Bold kinetic type breaking apart against a stark dark textured slate background.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Deepens the psychological consequence of the artistic mutilation shown in beat 125.
storyboard.addedInformation: Framing the destruction as internal psychological annihilation rather than mere censorship.

image.subject: In a high-ceilinged stone corridor of the Shanghai Conservatory in 1966, Zhuli: A graceful 19-year-old Chinese violinist with fiery expressive dark eyes, hair tied back with a simple red ribbon, slender hands calloused from violin strings, wearing a modest dark cotton student dress, stands rigid and unyielding clutching her wooden violin case while revolutionary student cadre pass by in the background.

storyboard.claim: Zhuli experiences the deepest tragedy because she refuses to compromise her musical integrity.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Zhuli standing motionless in sharp focus amidst passing blurred silhouettes of students.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Connects the cognitive dissonance directly to Zhuli's personal stance.
storyboard.addedInformation: Highlights her isolation and stubborn purity in a conforming collective.

image.subject: A warm vintage sepia-toned archival photograph from 1965 showing Zhuli: A graceful 19-year-old Chinese violinist with fiery expressive dark eyes, hair tied back with a simple red ribbon, slender hands calloused from violin strings, wearing a modest dark cotton student dress, smiling proudly while tuning her violin in the sunlight beside an ivy-covered Conservatory stone archway.

storyboard.claim: Zhuli chose silence over artistic compromise and paid with her life.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A framed archival portrait photograph of Zhuli preserved from before the Cultural Revolution.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Concludes the opening sequence on Zhuli's stance, foreshadowing her fate.
storyboard.addedInformation: Humanizes her youth and brilliance right before detailing the ordeal that killed her.

storyboard.claim: To understand Zhuli's fate requires examining the public struggle session at the conservatory.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Large kinetic typography posing the question against a dark blood-red tinted background.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Transitions from the overview of her death to the specific historical mechanism.
storyboard.addedInformation: Prepares the viewer for the harrowing breakdown of the struggle session ritual.

image.subject: In the expansive paved central courtyard of the Shanghai Conservatory of Music in 1966, dozens of student Red Guards wearing olive green military tunics and red fabric armbands gather in rows below tall stone building balconies hung with large crimson propaganda banners.

storyboard.claim: The struggle session was an extralegal spectacle of mass humiliation orchestrating student violence.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A wide cinematic photograph of the crowded Conservatory courtyard filled with uniforms and red banners.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Directly answers the transition in beat 129 by showing the struggle session setting.
storyboard.addedInformation: Clarifies that this was a mass ritual enforced by teenage students, not a court of law.

image.subject: From a second-story stone balcony overlooking the Shanghai Conservatory courtyard in 1966, a high-angle view captures a massive sea of students circling an empty wooden stool in the courtyard center beneath fluttering paper slogans and megaphone speakers.

storyboard.claim: The struggle session operated as a staged theatrical spectacle designed to crush individual psychology.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Balcony perspective looking down upon the intimidating concentric circle of accusers.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Expands on the nature of the struggle session as theatrical psychological warfare.
storyboard.addedInformation: Emphasizes the panoptic, arena-like staging where all eyes focus on one target.

image.subject: Across the threshold of the Shanghai Conservatory lecture hall in 1966, Zhuli: A graceful 19-year-old Chinese violinist with fiery expressive dark eyes, hair tied back with a simple red ribbon, slender hands calloused from violin strings, wearing a modest dark cotton student dress, is forcefully escorted forward by fellow music students wearing red fabric armbands and cadre jackets.

storyboard.claim: Zhuli is seized and dragged into the courtyard by the very classmates she studied music with.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Zhuli's stricken face as familiar student peers grip her arms and usher her toward the crowd.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Brings Zhuli into the center of the crowd described in beat 131.
storyboard.addedInformation: Underlines the betrayal of shared conservatory friendships turned into ideological hostility.

image.subject: On the rough gray concrete pavement of the Shanghai Conservatory courtyard in 1966, Zhuli: A graceful 19-year-old Chinese violinist with fiery expressive dark eyes, hair tied back with a simple red ribbon, slender hands calloused from violin strings, wearing a modest dark cotton student dress, is made to kneel surrounded by the dark leather boots and cloth shoes of surrounding student cadre.

storyboard.claim: Zhuli is forced onto the hard concrete courtyard before the assembled conservatory student body.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Low-angle shot focusing on Zhuli kneeling on coarse stone paving as feet encircle her.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the immediate physical subjugation following her dragging from the hall.
storyboard.addedInformation: Captures the visceral contrast between delicate musicianship and brutal concrete floor.

storyboard.claim: Analyzing the underlying psychological mechanics behind the public humiliation ritual.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Bold kinetic prompt asking what drives this specific psychological terror.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Pauses the scene at the moment of kneeling to dissect the underlying system.
storyboard.addedInformation: Invites analytical reflection on the mechanics of state totalitarian pressure.

storyboard.claim: The struggle session seeks not just corporal punishment, but voluntary complicity through public confession.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Structured typography checklist displaying the three progressive stages of totalitarian subjugation.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the question in beat 134 by defining the state's objective.
storyboard.addedInformation: Clarifies that ideological regimes require victims to assent to their own condemnation.

image.subject: In the Shanghai Conservatory courtyard in 1966, Zhuli: A graceful 19-year-old Chinese violinist with fiery expressive dark eyes, hair tied back with a simple red ribbon, slender hands calloused from violin strings, wearing a modest dark cotton student dress, kneels before a metal microphone placed on a small wooden table, her lips pressed tightly together in defiant silence while accusers point down at her.

storyboard.claim: The inquisitors demand that Zhuli verbally confess to being a bourgeois parasite.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The cold metal microphone thrust in front of Zhuli's silent, unyielding face.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Connects the theoretical checklist from beat 135 to Zhuli's specific trial.
storyboard.addedInformation: Depicts the microphone as an instrument of state absorption and coercion.

image.subject: A stark close-up photograph on the rain-dampened stone courtyard floor in 1966 showing a shattered wooden violin bow, frayed horsehair tangled among scattered paper leaflets and muddy footprints.

storyboard.claim: Physical degradation is calibrated to shatter the victim's spiritual independence first.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Discarded broken violin bow and shredded sheet music lying in courtyard mud.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Elaborates on the purpose behind the physical assault.
storyboard.addedInformation: Uses the broken instrument as a potent visual metaphor for crushed spiritual vitality.

image.subject: On the courtyard stones of the Shanghai Conservatory in 1966, rusty metal shears lie beside severed clumps of dark hair and large spatters of black Chinese calligraphy ink pooled across the pavement next to a kicked-over wooden stool.

storyboard.claim: Students cut off her hair with heavy scissors and throw black ink into her face to deface her.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Aftermath still-life of rusty shears, sheared hair strands, and viscous black ink on concrete.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Depicts the immediate physical details of the struggle session described in the narration.
storyboard.addedInformation: Focuses on evocative artifacts (ink, hair, shears) to convey trauma without violent gore.

image.subject: In the courtyard in 1966, Zhuli: A graceful 19-year-old Chinese violinist with fiery expressive dark eyes, hair tied back with a simple red ribbon, slender hands calloused from violin strings, wearing a modest dark cotton student dress, kneels with ink streaks across her cheeks, maintaining an unflinching dignified gaze while blurred background figures shout and brandish little red books.

storyboard.claim: The screaming crowd tries to dehumanize her with insults and black ink.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Zhuli's ink-marked face remaining composed and resolute amidst surrounding shouting faces.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows Zhuli bearing the ink and insults described in beat 138.
storyboard.addedInformation: Reveals her moral superiority and stillness against the frenzy of the mob.

image.subject: Against the brick wall of the Shanghai Conservatory in 1966, layers of massive white and red dazibao propaganda posters with ferocious hand-brushed Chinese characters brand students as bourgeois reactionaries and capitalist spies.

storyboard.claim: Vicious labels like capitalist spy and bourgeois rat are plastered across the conservatory walls.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Wall covered with dramatic, dripping ink slogans in Chinese script calling for denunciation.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Translates the auditory shouting into the physical environment of written accusations.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows how public architecture was weaponized into permanent slander.

storyboard.claim: The narrator wonders how anyone can endure such total humiliation without losing their mind.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Minimal stark typography questioning human psychological endurance under mob terror.
storyboard.onScreenText: WHAT IS GOING THROUGH HER HEAD?
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Reacts to the horror of the scene by questioning her inner survival mechanism.
storyboard.addedInformation: Frames the turning point from external assault to internal reality.

storyboard.claim: Why she didn't just give in and confess to stop the scissors.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Punchy, rhythmic kinetic text revealing that the answer lay in what she did internally.
storyboard.onScreenText: BECAUSE OF WHAT SHE DID INTERNALLY
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Builds suspense in answering the questions posed in beat 141.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets up Madeleine Thien's core literary revelation about interior resistance.

image.subject: In a quiet rainy Vancouver study in 1991, Marie: A 22-year-old Chinese-Canadian woman with intelligent observant dark eyes, shoulder-length straight black hair, wearing an oversized knit wool sweater and denim, studying handwritten notebooks at a wooden desk, turns the fragile pages of a hand-copied notebook under a warm desk lamp.

storyboard.claim: Madeleine Thien's novel uncovers the crucial psychological detail of Zhuli's silent rebellion.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Marie examining the handwritten testimony preserved in The Book of Records in Vancouver.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Transitions from the Shanghai flashback to the frame narrator studying the text.
storyboard.addedInformation: Connects Zhuli's interiority to Marie's act of reading and preservation decades later.

image.subject: A monochrome archival photograph capturing Zhuli: A graceful 19-year-old Chinese violinist with fiery expressive dark eyes, hair tied back with a simple red ribbon, slender hands calloused from violin strings, wearing a modest dark cotton student dress, kneeling on the wet stone courtyard in 1966, eyes gently shut in profound silent concentration while rain begins to fall.

storyboard.claim: Even while bleeding and humiliated on the concrete, Zhuli stages an internal rebellion.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Framed intimate portrait of Zhuli kneeling with eyes closed in serene inner concentration.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Returns to Zhuli kneeling on the courtyard floor from beat 143.
storyboard.addedInformation: Depicts her serene inner detachment from the violent outer world.

image.subject: A vintage close-up photograph of open classical violin score sheets featuring complex musical notation for Ravel's Tzigane and Prokofiev sonatas, illuminated by dramatic golden light against dark mahogany wood in an empty music hall.

storyboard.claim: Inside her mind on the concrete, Zhuli mentally plays Ravel's Tzigane and Prokofiev violin sonatas note for note.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Vivid close-up of intricate classical staves and rapid violin notes.
storyboard.onScreenText: PLAYING RAVEL AND PROKOFIEV IN HER MIND
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Reveals the exact content of her interior concentration in beat 144.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the virtuosity and complexity of the music she summons silently.

image.subject: In the quiet dim archive room of the Shanghai Conservatory in 1966, massive stacks of heavy leather-bound musical scores and bound symphonies are built up like high defensive walls on a long wooden reading table.

storyboard.claim: Zhuli builds an impregnable defensive fortress out of music in her consciousness.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Towering volumes of classical scores stacked like fortress battlements.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Visualizes the metaphor of building a fortress out of counterpoint.
storyboard.addedInformation: Gives solid, tangible form to the concept of psychological sanctuary.

image.subject: A luminous photograph looking down from the gallery into a majestic, empty European-style symphony hall with tiers of polished wood, golden acoustic panels, and an empty illuminated stage holding a single violin on a stand.

storyboard.claim: The domain of musical counterpoint within her becomes an impenetrable private sanctuary.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Empty, pristine illuminated acoustic hall glowing in warm amber light.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Expands on the nature of the fortress described in beat 146.
storyboard.addedInformation: Contrasts the chaotic, muddy courtyard outside with the pure architectural symmetry of music within.

image.subject: On a radiant concert stage bathed in brilliant warm spotlights, Zhuli: A graceful 19-year-old Chinese violinist with fiery expressive dark eyes, hair tied back with a simple red ribbon, slender hands calloused from violin strings, wearing a modest dark cotton student dress, plays her violin with sublime passion and immaculate poise before an imaginary auditorium.

storyboard.claim: Her persecutors can destroy her physical body, but they cannot touch the concert hall in her mind.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Zhuli performing with radiant freedom on an imagined stage.
storyboard.onScreenText: THE CONCERT HALL IN HER MIND
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Brings Zhuli into the center of the interior hall created in beat 147.
storyboard.addedInformation: Triumphantly depicts the inviolability of human artistic imagination.

image.subject: On a plain wooden desk in a Shanghai study in 1966, an antique brass mechanical metronome ticks beside an unvarnished spruce violin body and handwritten musical manuscript pages inscribed in black ink.

storyboard.claim: Classical music serves as Zhuli's irreducible anchor to her humanity and moral identity.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Still life of metronome, violin craftsmanship, and ink staves in soft morning light.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Synthesizes why the inner performance in beat 148 matters.
storyboard.addedInformation: Rooted in props that measure time, truth, and human discipline.

storyboard.claim: Uttering the required confession would allow the totalitarian collective to rewrite her soul.
storyboard.concreteVisual: High-contrast text stating that confession equals psychic colonization.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains why she refused to utter a single word to the mob.
storyboard.addedInformation: Emphasizes that speech under coercion is ideological surrender.

left.label: SILENCED
left.subject: A quiet, shadowed study in Shanghai in 1966 with an empty wooden music stand standing in front of closed curtains

right.label: RE-RECORDED
right.subject: A cold metal megaphone horn mounted atop a gray concrete utility pole blaring state slogans across a dusty courtyard

storyboard.claim: Being forced into silence is tragic, but being re-recorded in the state's voice is total spiritual annihilation.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Split screen comparing a silent solitary music stand with an abrasive propaganda loudspeaker.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Connects Zhuli's refusal to the philosophical core thesis of the video.
storyboard.addedInformation: Provides visual duality between natural human stillness and mechanized collective indoctrination.

image.subject: Along the exterior brick wall of a Shanghai Conservatory dormitory in 1966, a cluster of weathered industrial public-address horn speakers is mounted above tangled black cables beneath a heavy, overcast gray sky.

storyboard.claim: Speaking in the state's mandated voice constitutes the true death of the authentic self.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Ominous industrial horn speakers mounted high on institutional brickwork.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Deepens the 're-recorded' side of the comparison in beat 151.
storyboard.addedInformation: Emphasizes the ubiquitous physical apparatus of state surveillance and broadcast.

image.subject: In a quiet corner of a dimly lit attic room in Shanghai at dusk in 1966, Zhuli: A graceful 19-year-old Chinese violinist with fiery expressive dark eyes, hair tied back with a simple red ribbon, slender hands calloused from violin strings, wearing a modest dark cotton student dress, sits by an open window gazing out over gray tiled rooftops while silently pressing her fingers along her bare forearm as if playing violin fingerings.

storyboard.claim: By keeping Prokofiev playing silently in her head, Zhuli retains her authentic soul at the cost of life.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Zhuli sitting in twilight practicing silent fingerings along her arm by an attic window.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows her retreat into silent practice after the struggle session.
storyboard.addedInformation: Portrays the intimate physical habit of an instrumentless musician.

image.subject: A desaturated vintage archival photograph of an empty Shanghai Conservatory hallway in autumn 1966, lined with row upon row of battered, dented metal student instrument lockers under cold fluorescent tube lighting.

storyboard.claim: Physically shattered and recognizing that her world has vanished, Zhuli finds no place left for her.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Bleak, desolate perspective of the abandoned conservatory locker hallway.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Depicts the absolute institutional emptiness that followed her ordeal.
storyboard.addedInformation: Conveys the irreversible loss of the artistic home she loved.

image.subject: On a worn dark wooden tabletop in Shanghai in 1966, a torn scrap of coarse rice paper lies inscribed with delicate black brush calligraphy beside a dark ceramic inkstone and a bamboo brush.

storyboard.claim: Zhuli takes her own life, leaving behind a final note written on a scrap of paper.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Solemn macro photograph of the handwritten farewell note on torn rice paper.
storyboard.onScreenText: A NOTE ON A SCRAP OF PAPER
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Marks the decisive moment of her suicide.
storyboard.addedInformation: Substitutes graphic depiction of death with the quiet literary artifact of her last words.

image.subject: Looking through an open high wooden window frame of the Shanghai Conservatory into an immense autumn evening sky at twilight in 1966, with drifting purple and pale gold clouds stretching toward the western horizon above traditional tiled rooftops.

storyboard.claim: Zhuli steps into the western sky in an act of ultimate refusal against totalitarian complicity.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The vast, luminous western horizon seen from the elevated conservatory window.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Translates Thien's poetic phrase 'steps into the western sky' into visual space.
storyboard.addedInformation: Creates a transcendent, dignified sense of release rather than violent tragedy.

image.subject: A nostalgic black-and-white photograph in a paper mount from 1965 showing Zhuli: A graceful 19-year-old Chinese violinist with fiery expressive dark eyes, hair tied back with a simple red ribbon, slender hands calloused from violin strings, wearing a modest dark cotton student dress, laughing as she walks with her violin case across the Conservatory lawn.

storyboard.claim: Her choice represents a terrifying moral purity that haunts everyone left behind.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A preserved snapshot of Zhuli in her vibrant, joyful student prime.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Reflects on the moral magnitude of her suicide.
storyboard.addedInformation: Reminds the viewer of the human loss, making the ethical question sharper.

storyboard.claim: Her death leaves an agonizing moral dilemma for the surviving musicians in the room.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Typography highlighting the moral question facing those who survived.
storyboard.onScreenText: WHAT HAPPENS TO THOSE WHO REMAIN?
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Directly bridges Zhuli's sacrifice to the fate of the surviving characters.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets up the psychological conflict between martyrdom and survival.

image.subject: On a brightly lit auditorium stage in Shanghai in 1967, Kai: A charismatic 30-year-old Chinese pianist with sharp intense eyes, neat swept-back black hair, lean athletic frame, wearing a crisp dark wool tunic or pressed shirt, carrying an aura of guarded vigilance, sits upright at a black concert grand piano with hands poised above the keys under the watchful gaze of uniformed party officials seated in the front row.

storyboard.claim: Kai chooses the alternative path: playing the regime's game to stay alive.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Kai performing under bright lights under the watchful supervision of cadre.
storyboard.onScreenText: PLAYING THE GAME TO STAY ALIVE
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the question in beat 158 by introducing Kai's survival strategy.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the tense, guarded posture required to survive through compliance.

left.label: ZHULI: DEATH
left.subject: A quiet rain-washed window in an attic practice room in Shanghai with a closed violin case left alone on a wooden chair

right.label: KAI: SURVIVAL
right.subject: Kai: A charismatic 30-year-old Chinese pianist with sharp intense eyes, neat swept-back black hair, lean athletic frame, wearing a crisp dark wool tunic or pressed shirt, carrying an aura of guarded vigilance, standing bowed before state applause banners in a crowded municipal concert hall

storyboard.claim: The narrative shifts to Kai, contrasting Zhuli's unbending death with Kai's morally compromised survival.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Split composition contrasting Zhuli's abandoned violin case with Kai bowing to state officials.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Closes Chunk 4 by contrasting the two divergent paths of the young musicians.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets up the deep dive into Kai's collaboration, guilt, and legacy in the next act.
